The current governor of New York was never elected to the job. She got it because Andrew Cuomo was a predator who resigned in disgrace. Since then, she’s presided over the largest population exodus of any state, a migrant crisis she helped create, a $𝟐𝟔𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭 she can’t balance, and an approval rating so low that members of her own party are openly plotting to replace her. Here’s the full picture.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝: 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝐁𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐨 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐫’𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧

Born Kathleen Mary Courtney on August 27, 1958, in Buffalo, New York. Her father was a steelworker; the family lived in a 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐥 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 when she was young. Irish Catholic, working-class roots — and she talks about it constantly. She graduated from Syracuse University and earned a law degree from Catholic University in D.C., then worked as a corporate lawyer and Capitol Hill aide.

She served on the Hamburg Town Board, then as Erie County Clerk for 4 years. In 2011, she won a special election for Congress in a deep-red district — but lost it a year later when it was redrawn. After two years out of office, Andrew Cuomo plucked her from obscurity to be his running mate in 2014. She was chosen not for her talent but for her geography — a woman from upstate to balance a New York City governor. She served as lieutenant governor for seven years, a job she later admitted was largely ceremonial. “𝘐 𝘥𝘪𝘥𝘯’𝘵 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘬 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘢𝘱𝘪𝘵𝘰𝘭”, she told a reporter.

Then on August 24, 2021, Andrew Cuomo resigned after the New York Attorney General found he had sexually harassed 𝟏𝟏 𝐰𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧. Just like that, Kathleen Courtney Hochul — the woman nobody chose, nobody vetted, and nobody outside of Western New York had heard of — became the 57th governor of the state of New York. Not by election. By accident.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐔𝐩 𝐒𝐡𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝 — 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝

One of Hochul’s first acts as governor was to reveal what Cuomo had hidden: the state had undercounted COVID nursing home deaths by 𝟏𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎 — bringing the true toll to over 𝟏𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 elderly New Yorkers who died after Cuomo’s administration ordered COVID-positive patients back into nursing facilities (NY AG Report). It was the right thing to do. Cuomo’s cover-up was a scandal of historic proportions.

And then Hochul buried it. When the U.S. House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic investigated the nursing home deaths, Hochul’s administration 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 despite 𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐬 from Congress (House Select Subcommittee). She stonewalled a bipartisan investigation into the deaths of 15,000 elderly citizens. The same cover-up she exposed under Cuomo, she perpetuated under her own name. The families of those 𝟏𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐬 never got answers — not from Cuomo and not from Hochul.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐮𝐬𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐝: 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭

Hochul’s husband, 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐦 𝐇𝐨𝐜𝐡𝐮𝐥 𝐉𝐫., serves as 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐫 𝐕𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 — a multibillion-dollar hospitality and gaming conglomerate based in Buffalo. Delaware North operates casinos, stadiums, airports, and resorts across the country. The company has spent over $𝟑𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐛𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 Hochul’s office since she became governor (𝘛𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘜𝘯𝘪𝘰𝘯).

While her husband collected his salary from Delaware North, Hochul championed the most controversial stadium deal in New York history: a $𝟏.𝟒 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐲 for a new Buffalo Bills stadium — at the time the largest taxpayer contribution to a professional sports facility in American history. Delaware North operates the 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬’ 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐮𝐦. Her husband’s company directly profits from the deal she pushed through with public money. She has dismissed conflict-of-interest questions as “𝘴𝘦𝘹𝘪𝘴𝘵”.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐂𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬: $𝟒.𝟑 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠

When the migrant crisis hit New York in 2022, Hochul initially embraced it. New York was a “sanctuary” state. The city that never sleeps would welcome everyone. Then the bills arrived.

New York has allocated over $𝟒.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 for illegal immigrant services — housing, healthcare, food, legal aid (NY Comptroller). At the peak, the city was spending $𝟑𝟕𝟎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 to house migrants in hotels — nearly double the $𝟐𝟎𝟕 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 it spent to shelter its own homeless population. Think about that: illegal immigrants got better accommodations than American citizens sleeping on the streets.

By January 2025, the money ran out. Hochul cut off new funding for migrant services — after years of promising that the federal government would reimburse the state. The reimbursement never came. $𝟒.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 of New York taxpayer money, gone. Hotels converted to shelters. Schools overcrowded. Emergency rooms overwhelmed. And when it became politically untenable, she reversed course and pretended she’d been tough on the issue all along.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐄𝐱𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐬

People are leaving New York in droves. Between 2024 and 2025, New York lost a net 𝟏𝟑𝟕,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 to other states — the 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝-𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐰 𝐩𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 of any state in America (U.S. Census). A 𝟒𝟐% of those who left cited housing costs as the primary driver. Families, businesses, and tax revenue are fleeing to Florida, Texas, the Carolinas — anywhere that doesn’t tax you into poverty and then spend your money housing illegal immigrants in hotels.

This isn’t a blip. New York has lost congressional seats in two consecutive redistricting cycles because the population keeps shrinking. The state that was once the center of American gravity is hemorrhaging its own citizens, and Hochul has done nothing to reverse it.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠

text:
The Decline of Meritocracy in America’s Public Schools Today Started in San Francisco

In 2006, a consequential battle was raging in the heart of San Francisco for the soul of its public schools. On one side was Dr. Arlene Ackerman, the district’s first African American female superintendent and a graduate of Harris-Stowe Teachers College in St. Louis and Harvard University. 

She had tirelessly driven five straight years of test score gains across all racial cohorts. From 2004 to 2006, SFUSD was also the top performing urban school district in California, and in 2005 was nominated as a top 5 urban school district in the country by the Broad Foundation. For extra measure, during her first year on the job Dr. Ackerman exposed corruption in the school district, leading to more than $43 million in recoveries for public schools.

In any other city, a statue would be made in her honor. But in San Francisco, she was fired.

Opposing Dr. Ackerman were San Francisco progressives, in alliance with the teachers’ union. Their arguments for her dismissal centered around a vague accusation over her “confrontational style.” Ultimately, the progressives and teachers’ union won. On her way out, they refused her $170,000 in unpaid benefits while public figures and union leaders worked to tarnish her reputation.

I was there. From 2003 until my high school graduation in 2006, I sat on the Board of Education advocating for student interests. I often found myself wondering how our meetings focused more on distracting pet causes such as “banning irradiated meats” and “banning ROTC” than on the nuts and bolts of running a complex school system such as balancing the budget and holding teachers and schools accountable for student performance. Staff time and district resources were wasted trying to earn national headlines for progressive politicians aiming for higher office, rather than in serving students who needed help the most.

Afterwards, progressives and the local teachers union were the dominant force in San Francisco politics and in leading public schools. While centrists and moderates such as Jill Wynns and Dan Kelly were pushed out, several progressive school board members such as Jane Kim served on the Board of Supervisors from 2011-2019 and Hydra Mendoza became an advisor to Gavin Newsom.

Meanwhile, students suffered and families with means left the district. Since 2006, SFUSD’s enrollment fell from 55,000 to 49,000 by 2023, and math proficiency for Black students dropped to 16% in 2022, per state data. The district never again reclaimed its place as a top urban school district in California. Instead, under the leadership of the teachers union and progressives, magnet programs such as Lowell High School and Ruth Asawa School of the Arts, my alma mater, were constantly threatened and public school students were prevented from taking algebra in 8th grade.

Lacking a realistic understanding of how the world works and how to run a complicated educational bureaucracy, the progressive-led school district has faced ongoing challenges including budget deficits, declining enrollment, and achievement gaps. For example, SFUSD’s 2023 $400 million deficit forced school closures. Around that time, I also saw how the district repurposed funds clearly promised for one thing such as facilities improvements to hide problems in other areas such as the budget shortfall.

The sad truth is that more money will not solve these persistent, entrenched problems in the school district without new leadership.

For three years while on the SFUSD Board of Education, I saw Dr. Ackerman fight impossible battles to help all students in the school district improve. I saw one of the most inspiring educators of my lifetime kicked to the curb because not enough community members, parents and responsible adults stood up for her in the same way she stood up for us. Mark Sanchez, a core leader in Dr. Ackerman’s departure from SFUSD, returned to the Board of Education in 2020.

I also saw how the toxic mentality led by San Francisco progressives eventually spread around the country, influencing Seattle Public School’s 2024 shutdown of gifted programs, and changing the merit focus of magnet schools such as Thomas Jefferson High School in Virginia. A top mayoral candidate of New York City is advocating severe changes to some of the top public magnet schools in the country. 

The erosion of magnet programs and advanced coursework risks undermining America’s competitiveness, as fewer students access STEM pathways – particularly students who cannot afford private or supplementary programs outside public schools.

Despite five straight years of clear results, we abandoned Dr. Ackerman and the moderates of the San Francisco board in their fight for children against anti-merit progressives and political forces. Children are still facing the consequences to this day, while problems in education will likely show up in society long into the future.

To rebuild, we must restore meritocracy as the cornerstone of education policy, nurturing and empowering leaders who prioritize measurable outcomes over politics. Without this, the cracks in our education system will deepen, threatening United States competitiveness for generations.

text:
Apartments in high-rises are inherently anti-family
The more of them you build, the lower fertility will be.
(Please share!)

As we confront the low-fertility crisis that is enveloping most countries, we need to understand the very low birth rates of cities in particular. One of the first facts of demography, immediately evident in the data and true almost everywhere, is that fertility is lower in urban cores than anywhere else.

Economists like Bryan Caplan claim that fertility is so low in cities mainly because of cost. If cost is the main reason birth rates are so low among people living in urban high-rises, then we should double down and keep building more of them until apartments are affordable enough to give us the baby boom we so desperately need.

But if fertility in apartment towers is low because this type of housing is inherently negative for family formation, then building ever more high rises is a very bad idea, because over time an increasing share of people will live in an anti-natal housing type.

How can we find out which of these answers is correct? Randomized controlled trials are surely impossible for something like this.

Fortunately, a great natural experiment exists. East Asian countries have been constructing apartment towers like crazy. In an apartment-building frenzy, the number of dwellings per capita has grown by 10-17% across Asia as a chart published in 2023 by John Burn-Murdoch shows. Meanwhile the number of dwellings per capita has grown slowly in Europe and has been stagnant in the Anglosphere.

And this housing is affordable for young people. Incredibly, the homeownership rate of young people in China is twice the rate of the US. The second chart is from 2017, when the average millennial was just 28 or 29. Some 70% of young Chinese were homeowners in 2017, a number that may be even higher now after much more additional building.

With so much housing being built, Asia should be having an incredible baby boom right about now, right?

Unfortunately, exactly the opposite is happening as Asian fertility has completely collapsed. In 2023 the total fertility rate was 0.72 births per woman in South Korea, 1.02 in China, 1.20 in Japan, 0.75 in Hong Kong and 0.86 in Taiwan. By contrast the TFR was 1.62 in the United States, 1.56 in New Zealand and 1.52 in Ireland. These Anglosphere numbers are not great but still twice the fertility of those East Asian countries. (‘Replacement fertility’ is about 2.1 births per woman.)

Why isn’t all that building in Asia yielding more babies? If you have travelled in East Asian countries as I have, you know that the housing that is being built is almost entirely in the form of high-rise apartment towers.

Below is Shanghai, TFR 0.54. That is only around half of the (already very low) Chinese level. At that rate, for every 100 people there would be only around 6.25 grandchildren and 2 great-grandchildren. It isn’t hyperbole to say that such numbers suggest civilizational collapse.

The same story is true in Seoul (TFR 0.54), Beijing (TFR 0.66) and Bangkok (TFR 0.8). In every instance, birth rates in these cities where housing is mostly high-rise apartments is far lower than for each nation as a whole.

It is not about small apartment size
A popular theory is that the cause of low fertility is that apartments in Asia are small and if you built larger, family-sized apartments, things would be just fine.

Wondering about that, I searched and found this: “Using transactions data, Colliers estimates that the average gross private apartment size is between 88 and 98 square meters across Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.” That is 947-1054 square feet, substantially bigger than the average apartment size in the United States (882 square feet).

One of my Shanghai readers responded to a recent post by noting, “I actually live in Shanghai, and most new developments here start at 1800sf/3br.” Another replied, “Most apartments built post 2000 in Shanghai are 3+ beds.”

I don’t have the data on the exact mix being built, but it is clear that plenty of the apartments in Shanghai are sized for families, and yet its fertility is mind-bogglingly low even by Chinese standards.

Fertility is far lower in apartment towers for a whole host of reasons beyond size and cost
Economists are fixated on things like price and price per square foot. But there are whole lot of other factors that make high rise towers particularly bad for families.

· Noise and privacy issues. Apartment living means you share walls and common areas with many neighbors. Kids, meanwhile, are noisy, messy, and often embarrassing. Even one screaming kid will be an imposition on your neighbors when walls are shared. Imagine three or four!

· Lack of a yard for kids to play in. A typical single-family home has far more usable space than a comparably sized apartment because of the yard. (Our family residence for instance has 15,000 square feet of yard, a third of an acre, which greatly reduces the sense of crowding we would otherwise feel as a family of eight.)

· General crowding and density. Demographer Lyman Stone, in a June 2024 paper entitled More Crowding, Fewer Babies: The Effects of Housing Density on Fertility found that density (more people in a geographic area) and crowding (more people in one’s immediate space) both contribute to low fertility and when you have both, as you typically do in apartment blocks, you get exceptionally low fertility.

Fifty years ago, a few miles from where I write this, at the National Institutes of Mental Health in Bethesda, Maryland, John B. Calhoun conducted his famous ‘mouse utopia’ experiments. Calhoun found that even when mice have everything they need in terms of food and shelter, they won’t reproduce in conditions of high crowding and density. Humans seem to be a lot like mice in this regard. (His paper, titled Death Squared: The Explosive Growth and Demise of a Mouse Population, is riveting must-read because of how many of the neuroses of his mice seem to match what we see today, especially among people living in cities!)

None of these things would be made better by building more residential high-rises, and in many ways, conditions for families would be made worse!

Freeing up single family homes for young people? Hardly!
A few days ago, economist Scott Sumner tried to rebut arguments I raised on his blog TheMoneyIllusion:
“Some people argue that single family homes are better than high-rises for solving the fertility crisis. But even if that were true, it would help to build more high rises for single people and childless couples in places like LA, in order to free up more single-family homes for families with kids.”

@MattYglesias has made a similar argument responding my showing how anti-natal apartments tend to be.

Yet few older empty nesters giving are up their suburban houses to live in apartment towers. Instead, these apartment blocks draw mostly young people. My leafy DC suburb has many four- and five-bedroom houses occupied by only an older couple or even just a single widow. These houses would be perfect for a young family, but their older residents are mostly staying put.

It is possible that a few single-family homes may be freed up on the margins when you build high-rises, but mostly vast numbers of young people are enticed to live in apartments that are fundamentally anti-natal in character.

On a ten-day Japan trip with my family in September 2023 I saw a remarkable phenomenon where the building of apartment towers is leading to the loss of millions of single-family homes. Even though Japan is rapidly depopulating due to low birthrates, Tokyo is growing in population as it builds many high-rises and pulls young people in from across the country. Meanwhile millions of single-family homes across Japan, which would be perfect for families, are left vacant to decay. (Tokyo has the lowest fertility rate in all of Japan and constant building of residential high-rises in Tokyo drives what I have termed the Japanese Depopulation Conveyor belt of young people into the city!)

Building high-rise towers increases the share of people living in apartments, driving down fertility
If you plot the share of people living in apartments in a place against fertility, you find a robust negative relationship. The larger the share of people in a city that live in an apartment, the lower fertility will be. If you alter the mix of housing in the direction of more apartments, fertility will drop. This negative relationship is among the strongest evidence that apartments themselves are relatively anti-natal.

This relationship also holds on a national level. The greater the share of a country’s households that live in apartments, the lower its fertility rate will be. Spain, where around 70% of households live in apartments, has far lower fertility (1.13) than Australia (between 1.5 and 1.6), where only 15% live in apartments.

Since housing will be around generations to come, altering a country’s housing mix in the direction of apartments will have a particularly disastrous effect on birth rates in the long term. That seems like a very bad idea when demographic collapse is the risk we face.

Building housing is important, but that should mean quality single-family homes, not apartments in towers
House affordability matters a great deal for birth rates, as my own work shows. State-by-state, fertility is much higher when housing is more affordable in relation to local incomes. The economists are not wrong about this.

But housing type matters greatly for fertility, and most economists skip that part. Bryan Caplan’s 2024 graphic novel Build Baby Build is filled with pictures that look just like the above image of Shanghai. I know Caplan - he and his wife did not raise their family in environs like that. They raised their family in a single-family home in the tree-lined DC suburbs, as did other economists now advocating that we throw out limitations on height. Most of them have little appreciation for what that means.

(I met Caplan and discussed this topic one-on-one with him for more than an hour in a Zoom -- though he has refused so far to debate me publicly. He was friendly but said he would be convinced only if I could come up with the perfect analysis that matches every other variable – especially price per square foot for houses and apartments in the same place, good luck to me! I think the evidence that apartments in towers are anti-natal is already overwhelming.)

We can’t ignore the lessons of places like South Korea. After the Korean war, Korea saw a housing shortage and so began building big apartment buildings. Korea never stopped building them, and now around three in four Koreans lives in an apartment in a high rise - perhaps the highest rate of any country. This has contributed to the lowest fertility of any nation in the world, just 0.72. Korea will have a very difficult time raising birth rates, since all that anti-natal housing will be with them for generations to come. If trends continue, the demise of South Korea is in sight, and the wrong type of housing will be a big part of that story.

Everyone else should avoid making the same mistakes as East Asia has, by building in a way that helps and not hurts birth rates. (Many other factors matter too, like marriage, religiosity/culture and workism. I write plenty about those too.)

Please follow @MoreBirths for more on the global fertility crisis and how we can solve it.

Also see the thread that follows for many of my posts and threads on housing, density and birth rates.

text:
High prices are not the main cause of low fertility rates in cities
And building more urban high rises will likely lower, not raise fertility rates by drawing more people into those cities

I have written frequently about the relationship between high housing density* and low fertility. The most common counter argument is that the real problem is urban prices. Some claim that if you build more in cities, you will lower prices and get an urban baby boom. Economics professor Bryan Caplan and journalist @mattyglesias are both sympathetic to this idea and it seems logical.

Unfortunately, that is not what we see. Instead, we see incredibly low birthrates in dense cities even when prices are not the issue.

Macau, projected TFR of 0.49 in 2024 🤯

In the last week we were treated to the shocking news that Macau's fertility is down another 16% in 2024, which if the trend holds will mean a TFR of 0.49. This is probably the lowest fertility humanity has ever seen in peacetime.

For some this is proof that urban costs are too high. But lo, apartments in Macau are not expensive at all! In fact, Macau is incredibly affordable!
Macau's GDP per capita is $70,000 in nominal terms and $125,000 by purchasing power parity (Wiki). This is comparable to New York.  But rents in Macau are 72% lower than in New York!

If Macau's rents are low and easily affordable for most residents, how can they have such low birthrates? Density is a big part of the reason.

At 22,870 inhabitants per km², Macau is the densest jurisdiction in the world, denser than Singapore which itself suffers ultra-low fertility. Virtually everyone in Macau lives in an apartment tower. Studies (see below for a thread reviewing the literature) find that density is linked to low fertility, so perhaps we shouldn't be surprised if the densest place on Earth also has the lowest birthrates.

Tokyo, center of Japan's depopulation conveyor belt

Tokyo, Japan, provides a great natural experiment. What happens when you build urban high-rise towers in abundance? We once thought of Tokyo as expensive, but that is no longer true. Apartment towers have been added to the Tokyo skyline at a rapid clip, making it eminently affordable for young people.

Was there a baby boom? As Tokyo grew its housing stock and dramatically brought down home prices, did Tokyo residents suddenly start having more children? No, they are having fewer. Fertility in 2024 will almost certainly be under 1 in Tokyo, a catastrophe considering the government's desperation to raise birthrates.

But it is worse than this. Tokyo is the center of what I call the Japanese depopulation conveyor belt. The fertility in Tokyo is substantially lower than any other place in the country. But is Tokyo depopulating? No, it is growing as young people stream in from all over Japan, moves made possible by the abundance of new apartment towers. 

Meanwhile millions of houses in the beautiful Japanese countryside, which would be wonderful for raising big families, sit empty and abandoned. They can't compete with the lights of the city at the foot of Mt. Fuji.

Australia, where the pricey suburbs are much more fertile

Is this just something peculiar about East Asian fertility, irrelevant to the rest of the world? No. In fact, Australia provides a wonderful case of contrasts, between low fertility urban areas and high fertility American-style suburbs.

The thing to know about Australia is that its suburbs are not cheap but incredibly expensive. Here we can see the examples of greater Sydney, Bisbane, Melbourne and Perth, in maps courtesy of user NoneBusinessHey here on X.

Fertility rates in Australian urban cores, which consist largely of apartments and especially tall tower blocks, are at ultra-low levels. Meanwhile in the family friendly subdivisions around these cities, fertility rates are almost twice as high! This even though pricey suburban homes in Australia are usually the more expensive option compared to city apartments.

New Zealand may not show what people think it does

New Zealand is hailed as a success story for "upzoning", as a country of suburbs has started to build apartment towers and embrace density.

In 2015, when zoning laws were changed, the fertility of New Zealand was 2.0. By 2023, the TFR had fallen to 1.56, the fastest drop among the Anglosphere countries. Correlation is not causation, but that is not looking like success so far.

Housing type and density levels, more than prices, are the main drivers of low urban fertility

Demographer Lyman Stone has described how density seems to cause low fertility. Also, we can look at the rate of apartment living in different cities and different countries around the world. It turns out that the higher the share living in an apartment, the lower the birth rate, and the curve is steep!

This makes sense to anyone who has been a parent trying to raise children in an apartment. It feels awful as a parent when your noisy children are bothering the neighbors through the walls at all hours. It is difficult to entertain young kids all day when there is no yard for them to play in. It is nerve racking knowing the ever-present danger of a high balcony for little ones.

High prices are temporary as birth rates plunge
But if we rush to build dense apartment towers, they will drag down fertility for many generations to come

We are at a juncture when housing is difficult to afford for young people. Millennials are competing for houses with their parents, the Baby Boomers. We should do more to help them buy homes and form families! 

But the answer cannot be to build ever more anti-natal housing into the teeth of a low fertility crisis. Housing, once built lasts for many generations, so new housing should be of a family-friendly type (something with a yard for kids to play in) if we are to have a viable future!

After the war, Korea saw a housing crisis and resolved to build huge apartment towers as fast as possible. China too has gone the path of ultra-dense apartment blocks. Now both countries are stuck in an ultra-low fertility regime. They desperately try to pivot to higher birth rates, but their built housing stock dooms them. Young people in both countries are drawn to low fertility city life, and the depopulation conveyor belt runs hot.

We shouldn't make the same mistake.

* Yes, I know that density is not the only fertility factor. Religiosity, marriage norms and other factors matter too (and I write plenty about those). But density is amenable to public policy in a way that most other factors are not, and so it is worthy of special attention.

(Follow and share @MoreBirths, which is focused on solutions to the low birth rate crisis, the greatest challenge of our age.)

text:
“Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.”

This is so on point. Many Americans rightly think cities aren’t for families…but that’s because we stopped BUILDING them for families.

And while I do appreciate much of the YIMBY message (net good), I also think we need to be critical about what KIND of housing we are building. Not all housing is good housing. 

A city of only multi-family apartment buildings (as they’re built today) isn’t a city. It’s a collection of human storage units. 

That’s not to say big apartments are bad. But that ONLY big apartments are bad (which is virtually all new housing construction outside of suburban homes). 

Cities need design, beauty and humanity etched into every nook and cranny we can. And part of that beauty and humanity is incorporating children and families. 

Anecdotal, but something I’ve noticed holds generally true: If you make a place cool for kids and their parents (where both enjoy being there) it suddenly becomes a place for everyone—even the teens, singles and empty-nesters. I think there is something about having children around that can be life-giving and wholesome and bring out the best in people. 

To conclude: 

1) Hardware dictates what kind of software can run, and we’ve built hardware that’s incompatible for families in our cities.  

2) The built world is the human habitat. We shouldn’t treat it so flippantly as to simply say “anything that adds housing is good”. We actually do need GOOD housing. 

That doesn’t make it easy, and we shouldn’t be puritanical about it. There are real obstacles and limitations, and progress isn’t linear. But it SHOULD be the vision.

quote.text:
Very pleased to have contributed to the first issue of this new venture with @voxdotcom & @Arnold_Ventures: How Cities became places for the wealthy and/or childless … but how we can change that, by building housing designed FOR young couples and families.

My mission is to build housing for Families so people can have kids and stay in the City they love

I believe a primary reason people delay having a baby isn’t (just) culture and it's certainly not preference: It’s that the “cost” of doing so is moving out of your neighborhood, or out of the City entirely. Cities make it easy to be a young professional and extremely difficult to imagine being a parent.

And that matters far beyond individual families.
Seeing kids in a city signals something powerful to everyone else:

 "You can have kids here. It actually works."

That visibility lowers the psychological barrier to family formation. The same way seeing dogs tells you a neighborhood is pet-friendly. Kids also support the essential civic institutions cities need to thrive, especially public schools.

But developers today are mostly great at building two things: apartment buildings and mass planned single-family communities. They are not good at building the “missing middle” housing, the formats that actually fit the life stage when people are deciding whether they can stay in their neighborhood and start a family.

That’s the gap I want to fill.

I’m designing and building homes specifically for couples who love their neighborhood and want to feel comfortable enough to stop trying not to have kids:
Small 3BR/2BA rowhouses, 2BR/1BA apartments.

Baby Maybe housing: Homes with just enough space, one extra room, and the confidence that you could have a baby without being forced to leave everything you’ve built your life around.

And after that first baby becomes a toddler, the decision for a family to stay will depend on schools, parks, transit, childcare, and safety. But in that crucial first stage, when babies are small and when a couple is asking whether parenthood fits into city life, having the right kind of home can be literally life-changing.

Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.

La fertilité est fondamentalement mimétique : on veut des enfants parce qu’on en voit autour de nous. Quand on voit des enfants/bébés c’est assez irrésistible !

Israël démontre ce mécanisme : exposition constante aux familles nombreuses -> désir mimétique d’en avoir soi-même. Les communautés Haredi dont la fertilité élevée contamine progressivement le reste de la société israélienne.

Le danger c’est un cercle vicieux mortel dans les pays à basse fertilité :
Moins d’enfants -> Moins d’exposition sociale aux bébés -> Moins de désir d’enfants -> Encore moins de naissances -> Vieillissement accéléré -> Société de plus en plus hostile aux familles (infrastructures, normes, attentes) -> Encore moins d’enfants !

La Corée du Sud (TFR 0,8), Taïwan (0,7) et le Japon illustrent cette spirale : dans les grandes villes croiser un enfant devient exceptionnel. Les « childless cities » deviennent la norme. Quand toute votre cohorte est sans enfant……. avoir un bébé devient un acte socialement déviant plutôt que normal.

La société devient même hostile aux enfants : zones « no kids » dans les avions, hôtels « garantis sans enfants », invisibilisation croissante dans l’espace public. L’intolérance sociétale aux enfants accélère leur raréfaction.

Briser ce cercle vicieux exige des interventions culturelles massives (comme en Géorgie) ET structurelles (logement, garde d’enfants, transferts). Mais plus on attend plus c’est difficile : la norme sociale pro-famille s’évapore génération après génération !

Sans enfants pas d’avenir. Agissons avant qu’il ne soit trop tard !!

I'm all for enforcing laws (especially traffic laws), but the idea that aggressive law enforcement is necessary to entice suburban families back to US cities is implausible. 
 Let's consider Vienna (large city, demographically diverse, very dense):
Vienna has a MARKEDLY lower rate of violent crime than even our safest cities (NYC, Boston, SF, etc.).* Vienna does NOT have aggressive policing. At all. 
Vienna DOES stand out as a city where middle-income households remain in the core, thanks to family-friendly housing and walkable neighborhoods (it has courtyard urbanism).**
What do you think would happen to Vienna's crime rate if the 1M+ people making up its middle class decamped for suburbs, leaving wealthy professionals, low-wage service workers, and the unemployed? 
US cities have higher crime rates NOT because they lack law enforcement, but because all the generally law-abiding, nonviolent middle-income families left for the suburbs. 
Subtracting this population from the urban denominator obviously makes the urban crime rate greater as a statistic. But, also, subtracting this population from the city decreases the "eyes on the street" and the kind of people who tend to be engaged in the organic community safety activities that make neighborhoods safe even without aggressive policing. 

*Vienna has violent crime rate at 0.73 per 1,000 residents, compared to San Francisco (6.3), Boston (6.0), and New York City (6.7).
*About 68% of Vienna’s population is in a “medium income” bracket defined somewhat generously (60-180% of Vienna’s median).

text:
China has an abundance of inexpensive urban housing, and a TFR of just 1.02 in 2023

An important debate affecting the future of housing and birth rates in the United States is happening here on Twitter/X. @bryan_caplan, an influential libertarian economist, has a new book Build Baby Build that particularly urges housing deregulation in the direction of urban densification. 

Caplan claims that nobody really knows if urban density is a problem for birthrates because it might be just an artifact of city prices. (Conversely, I am under the impression that the urbanization/low fertility relationship is something like a first principle of demography, true everywhere in the world since Roman times.)

The debate matters because most of the world (including the US) is headed toward steep demographic decline.

To be fair, Caplan is quite correct that we need to build more housing. And he's been wonderful in other ways writing about solving the low birthrate crisis, including the book Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids. (My own pronatalist book still lies in the future!)

But when it comes to building, it matters greatly that new building be of a family-friendly type (especially single-family homes and townhomes) that will actually help families to have more children. Since housing, once built, endures for generations, getting this right is paramount for our future.

Caplan says in a podcast (just posted, see below),
"The papers [showing that higher density is associated with lower fertility] are making a good point. It is one that we should be thinking about. But they are really jumping the gun because normally high density and high prices go hand in hand.

We'd really need to be finding places where there's high density, but housing is really cheap. 

And that's really hard to find because why? Well, normally anytime you actually get a city then regulation is going to be fairly strict, so you don't get to observe this alternate universe. There may be somewhere on Earth, but that would be where you'd want to start.

As far as I can tell, the people that are getting worried about this haven't done that basic homework of trying to disentangle price from density.

You can imagine an area that's very dense and yet the housing is cheap so that someone that wants to go and have a lot of living space can and we just don't see that."

Actually, I had a post exactly one week ago that gave a number of examples (including of Tokyo, Japan) where abundant and cheap urban high-rises have not boosted fertility at all. The post, linked below, is entitled, 
"High prices are not the main cause of low fertility rates in cities 
And building more urban high rises will likely lower, not raise fertility rates"

I hope Bryan Caplan saw that post (which has had more than 100K views so far), since he clearly takes into account my other posts. But if he did, Caplan seems to ignore its substance, including several examples of affordable, high-density places, all of which are associated with extremely low birth rates.

Apartments in China are cheap and available

If you look at the averages, apartments in China are remarkably inexpensive.

"Today China is a country of homeowners with more than 90% of households owning homes (87% in urban and 96% in rural China) (Clark, Huang, & Yi, 2019). At the same time, more than 20% Chinese households own multiple homes, higher than many developed nations" (Huang et al., 2020)

China has such an abundance of urban high-rise units, that the average number of owned homes per household is greater than 1! And that was four years ago. There are now doubt many more apartment towers now!

Above, apartment towers in Shanghai and Tianjin (h/t BoredPanda).

(Admittedly, there are places in China where housing is incredibly expensive, but apartments over Central Park in NYC can cost $50 million. That doesn't mean housing isn't affordable generally.)

Meanwhile, fertility in China is incredibly low, especially in the urban areas

Has all this dense, cheap urban housing boosted birthrates? Not in least. The TFR across China was officially 1.02 in 2023, but it was far lower in the denser cities: just 0.72 in Beijing and 0.65 in Shanghai. 
A calamity for China and a disaster for the future of the global economy.
What is the problem? Part of it is, big apartment blocks strongly discourage family formation.

It seems to be down to the experience of density

A study in Finland (Kulu et al. 2007) found that fertility is much lower for residents of apartments than for residents of single-family homes.
Keep in mind, these effects were seen Finland at nowhere near the density of big apartment blocks.

Does this replicate in the United States? Yes, it does. The American Community Survey (2021) revealed that fertility rates for single family/townhomes were 1.95/1.93 respectively. But for apartment blocks of 20-49 units and greater than 50 units, the fertility rates were just 1.39/1.33 respectively. 

Of course, these Finnish and American studies don't mention price, but nobody thinks the average apartment in either instance would be costlier than a single-family home.

I'd love to directly debate Bryan Caplan on this

Caplan and I agree on a lot. We both agree that approving more single-family homes would be great for fertility. We both agree as well that young adults being able to move out of their parents' home and get a place of their own would be a very good thing for birthrates.

But the housing density issue is of great importance, and America needs to get it right. Whatever gets built will be around much longer than either of us, so it had better not be of an anti-natal type.

So far Caplan has declined to debate me directly, but hope springs eternal! In any case, addressing these issues is crucial.

text:
Almost every urban school district is facing a large, structural budget deficit due to declining enrollment and the end of COVID stimulus funds that requires very tough political decisions like Seattle made this week, else bankruptcy and/or state takeover looms.

Some districts will be able to address their deficits through job cuts in the near term, but almost all will eventually need to close schools, perhaps the most politically fraught action possible. School boards that refuse to do so won't be financially viable.

The enrollment decline in urban districts is almost universal and driven by a number of factors including bad demographics, rising housing prices that force low income families to the suburbs, growing preference for charters and home school, and chronic absenteeism.

Even growing metropolitan areas see their urban district shrinking. Houston ISD is -13% from 2019; Austin ISD is -9%. The school choice movement in red states will exacerbate this trend.

This trend has been brewing for years, but federal stimulus funding since 2020 has masked over the problem. With these funds ending this year, districts are waking up to 4 years of rising costs and falling enrollment with no backstop.

Districts all knew this fiscal cliff was coming, yet almost none prepared for it. The difficulty of government to address a crisis in advance is universal. School boards must make some very unpopular decisions. The question is whether they will.

text:
Economists like @bryan_caplan claim that the low fertility in cities is really due to high urban prices. And even if rents seem cheap, he claims, they aren't really cheap because the price per square foot is high.

Zvi Mowshowitz echoed the sentiment in a recent fertility roundup. "When you build a large apartment building, you lower the cost of housing everywhere, which is good for fertility in any given location. But the particular location is likely to be expensive, and thus locally have lower fertility, again partly via selection. If South Korea had twice as many high rises, allowing all units to be larger at lower prices, then the fertility penalty would stop."

But that thinking is all wrong.

I looked specifically at price per square foot. RentCafe presented 'the 30 most magnetic cities in the world' with information on cost per square foot so I used all cities on the list without any selection on my part.
The first observation is that fertility is incredibly low in almost every urban center, less than 1.2 on average.

But more importantly, price isn't the cause of low urban fertility and making housing cheap doesn't fix it. It turns out in Seoul (TFR 0.56 in 2024), Beijing (TFR 0.70) and Shanghai (TFR 0.61) rents are very low per square foot, just 20% of what they are in London, San Francisco and Manhattan.

These places have *already* followed the prescription in Caplan's Build Baby Build. They already built more than anyone else and housing is now cheap. You can get 1400 square feet in Seoul and 1700 square feet in Shanghai for the price of 300 feet in New York or London. Or (and this is more likely) you can get a cute little one-person apartment for almost nothing.
For all their building, were these cities rewarded with higher fertility? No! These cities ended up with some of the lowest fertility rates in recorded history!

What's going on?

To begin with low urban fertility is not fundamentally due to price: It is due to housing forms and density levels that are antinatal. 
https://t.co/AAJsnI5rJb

The problem is the housing itself. High rise apartments are poorly suited for families. Most have few bedrooms, no yard to play in, and noisy kids bother the neighbors.
Single-family homes, by contrast, are associated with far higher fertility. America’s Baby Boom coincided with a huge housing transformation as America went from being a nation of urban renters to a nation of suburban homeowners. Countries like Korea and China are doing the opposite of what gave us the Baby Boom.

Cheap Apartments = More Singles?
But why is the relationship negative? Why is fertility even lower in cities where housing costs less per square foot?

There is one intriguing explanation I have heard. It may be that cheap apartments in Korea and China actually encourage singlehood. Why does a young woman in Korea or China even need a man? She can have a stylish one-bedroom or studio for just a few hundred dollars a month!

Different housing types have vastly different impacts on fertility
The United States is dominated by single family zoning. Libertarians like Caplan and Ilya Somin think that is a problem. In fact, we are incredibly lucky to have rules that stop us from going over a cliff like China and Korea have.

Caplan and Somin think they have stumbled upon the holy grail of economic growth, unrestrained housing density. Bro!

2/2

Please share! And follow for more on how we can solve this crisis!

text:
Cities will always be a magnet for the ambitious and adventurous. They’re great places to be young ... as long as you don’t have kids.

That tension is at the heart of @rcobooth’s great Vox piece today, which explains how cities grew by attracting young millennials, but lost sight of the next step in most people’s lives. And now that oversight is becoming a crack in the foundation of urban America.

My mission is to build housing for Families so people can have kids and stay in the City they love

I believe a primary reason people delay having a baby isn’t (just) culture and it's certainly not preference: It’s that the “cost” of doing so is moving out of your neighborhood, or out of the City entirely. Cities make it easy to be a young professional and extremely difficult to imagine being a parent.

And that matters far beyond individual families.
Seeing kids in a city signals something powerful to everyone else:

 "You can have kids here. It actually works."

That visibility lowers the psychological barrier to family formation. The same way seeing dogs tells you a neighborhood is pet-friendly. Kids also support the essential civic institutions cities need to thrive, especially public schools.

But developers today are mostly great at building two things: apartment buildings and mass planned single-family communities. They are not good at building the “missing middle” housing, the formats that actually fit the life stage when people are deciding whether they can stay in their neighborhood and start a family.

That’s the gap I want to fill.

I’m designing and building homes specifically for couples who love their neighborhood and want to feel comfortable enough to stop trying not to have kids:
Small 3BR/2BA rowhouses, 2BR/1BA apartments.

Baby Maybe housing: Homes with just enough space, one extra room, and the confidence that you could have a baby without being forced to leave everything you’ve built your life around.

And after that first baby becomes a toddler, the decision for a family to stay will depend on schools, parks, transit, childcare, and safety. But in that crucial first stage, when babies are small and when a couple is asking whether parenthood fits into city life, having the right kind of home can be literally life-changing.

Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.

text:
Difficult Questions for Solving the Fertility Crisis
A discussion with arguably the greatest family thinker of our time

I was fortunate to have a great hour-long sit-down with @BradWilcoxIFS in the beautiful courtyard of the Rayburn House Office Building in DC yesterday, following a speech he gave. University of Virginia Professor Brad Wilcox is (among many other things) a founder of the Institute for Family Studies which has produced some of the most important work on issues that impact family formation.

Although Wilcox’s first focus is on marriage, our conversation covered a whole range of issues around birthrates.

I think the most interesting part of our discussion was where we hit snags. As we talked, we ran into some difficult problems where we do not yet have great answers. If we can figure these out, we can go a long way toward solving the fertility crisis.

(1) How can we address the density problem and incentivize people to spread out more?

Urbanization is a big root of the birthrate crisis. Cities are magnets for both economic and social reasons, but cities end up having incredibly low birthrates.

In Asia the problem is especially acute. Cities like Shanghai, Beijing, and Seoul all have fertility rates far below 1 birth per woman, as density, the entertainments of city life and the predominance of large apartment towers all conspire to hurt family formation. Yet even as rural areas empty out, cities become ever more crowded. Young people are drawn to urban cores, and then have very few children there.

In many countries struggling with too-low birthrates, including Japan, Korea, Spain and the United States, there are vast areas that sit neglected, where housing is cheap and space for families is abundant.

How can we encourage people, governments, and companies to spread out, and form new towns and especially to revitalize towns and smaller cities that are already there?

This is not a new problem but a very old one. For example, London has been a population sink for rural England throughout history. In theory the pressures to urbanize should be less because of communication networks and the Internet, but densification continues in most countries.

Wilcox suggested work-from-home and self-driving cars (enabling longer commutes) as two things that will help. True! But overall, we have no good answers to this so far.

(2) How can we introduce pro-family content into schools?

In his speech that preceded our conversation, entitled The Closing of the American Heart about the decline of marriage in America, Wilcox emphasized the need to teach young people both about the value of marriage and fertility time constraints.

We agree that education of young people is in a way the most obvious starting point for turning around the birthrate crisis. But as University of Maryland economist Melissa Kearney has noted, there is a taboo about talking about the value of marriage, even as its benefits for families are extraordinary.

How we persuade educators to teach pro-marriage and pro-natal content in high schools in colleges given the present political and social climate?

A difficult problem indeed!

(3) How can we get the left of the political spectrum to recognize and focus on the birthrate crisis?

Where are the left-wing pronatalists, I ask. Wilcox mentions Matthew Yglesias and I do admit that the author of One Billion Americans surely qualifies. But there don't seem to be a lot of others on the left. When I attended the Natalism Conference in Austin, Texas in December, I found myself wishing the political slant of most pronatalists wasn’t so obvious!

If pronatalism becomes coded as right-wing (and that is happening already) then left will be decidedly uninterested. That is a big problem when a majority of young women vote left.

We are already seeing a big political divide on birthrates, a divide that didn’t exist a generation ago.

(4) Who will lead the kinds of large scale pronatal movements we need and what organizations will appear to advocate pronatalism?

Given the civilizational impacts of collapsing fertility, it is surely the most under-emphasized problem in the world today. There are thousands of organizations and hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to environmental issues but what organizations and prominent leaders are dedicated to solving the truly existential low fertility crisis?

The Institute for Family Studies just launched a Pronatalism Initiative led by brilliant demographer Lyman Stone, but Wilcox tells me that is still just a one-man policy shop. I was surprised to learn IFS overall consists of just a few full-timers -- surely there should be hundreds at least! Can Professor Wilcox lead something much, much bigger? He tells me his plate is full, but we can only hope!

Where are the prominent pronatal leaders in the English-speaking world? If a young person is interested in helping to solve the low birthrate crisis, where can they even go right now? There should be several big pronatalist organizations, representing every perspective and political persuasion, to help turn things around.

So, consider these to be some of the great problems to solve at the center of the birthrate crisis. This is not an exhaustive list, but it is already a lot to work on. Make progress on any of these and you will make the world of the future a much, much better place!

But no city sustains great public spaces without excellent private housing options. 

If families can’t access well-designed homes with usable outdoor space (yards, courtyards, safe play areas), they’ll leave for the suburbs when kids arrive. Their tax dollars follow—funding suburban schools, rec centers, and sprawl infrastructure instead of city parks, plazas, transit, and public programming.

That’s why cities must prioritize housing typologies that deliver high-quality private outdoor access at urban densities: perimeter blocks, courtyard apartments, missing-middle forms. 

These retain middle-class families, grow the tax base, and create the political and fiscal will for ambitious public investments.

text:
Editorial: Sanctuary Cities Are Bleeding America Dry.
By Jon Fetherston 

Sanctuary cities were sold to the public as “compassion.” What they’ve become is chaos, draining hospitals, crippling schools, blowing up public safety budgets, and driving up car insurance rates for every law-abiding taxpayer. Enough is enough. It’s time to call these policies what they are: reckless, dangerous, and unsustainable.

Hospitals in sanctuary cities are drowning. Emergency rooms are packed, resources stretched thin, and staff burned out. Why? Because non-citizens, including those here illegally, use ERs as primary care and under federal law, hospitals can’t turn them away.
Every ambulance ride, every doctor’s visit, every surgery, it’s funded by you, the taxpayer. And while politicians pat themselves on the back for being “welcoming,” hospital wait times grow longer, and costs skyrocket. It’s no wonder hospitals in cities like Boston, New York, and Chicago are sounding the alarm: they can’t survive under this financial strain.

Walk into any public school in a sanctuary city and you’ll see overcrowded classrooms and teachers stretched beyond their limits. Districts are forced to hire translators, aides, and specialists, all without additional funding from the state or federal government.
Test scores decline. Resources for American students dry up. And special education and advanced placement programs,designed to help students with unique needs or exceptional abilities, are cut back to cover the costs of rapid, unchecked enrollment spikes.

Sanctuary policies don’t just make cities less safe, they bankrupt them. Local law enforcement is forbidden from cooperating with federal immigration officials, leaving dangerous criminals on the streets. Police departments are forced to spend more time, more money, and more manpower tracking repeat offenders that ICE could have deported.
Overtime budgets explode. Morale collapses. And when violence spikes from gang activity to drug trafficking city leaders have the audacity to claim “more funding” is the answer, when the real problem is their refusal to enforce the law.

Here’s the dirty little secret no politician wants to admit: sanctuary city policies drive up car insurance rates.
Unlicensed, uninsured drivers, often undocumented, cause accidents. The costs don’t disappear; they get shifted onto the people who follow the rules. If you’ve wondered why your premium jumped hundreds of dollars in the last two years, look no further than the flood of unqualified, unlicensed drivers on the road.
In cities and states that hand out driver’s licenses to illegal migrants, the problem only gets worse. It’s a tax, not on the wealthy, but on the working class.

Sanctuary cities are not compassionate. They’re not safe. And they’re not sustainable. They drain resources from hospitals and schools, balloon public safety costs, and make everyday life more expensive for the families who built these communities.

Politicians like Mayor Michelle Wu, Governor Maura Healey, and their allies know this. But they don’t care. They’d rather pander to activists and score political points than protect their own citizens.

Enough. It’s time to demand accountability. Repeal these reckless policies. Protect your hospitals. Protect your schools. Protect your neighborhoods. And start putting taxpayers first again.

Very pleased to have contributed to the first issue of this new venture with @voxdotcom & @Arnold_Ventures: How Cities became places for the wealthy and/or childless … but how we can change that, by building housing designed FOR young couples and families.

My mission is to build housing for Families so people can have kids and stay in the City they love

I believe a primary reason people delay having a baby isn’t (just) culture and it's certainly not preference: It’s that the “cost” of doing so is moving out of your neighborhood, or out of the City entirely. Cities make it easy to be a young professional and extremely difficult to imagine being a parent.

And that matters far beyond individual families.
Seeing kids in a city signals something powerful to everyone else:

 "You can have kids here. It actually works."

That visibility lowers the psychological barrier to family formation. The same way seeing dogs tells you a neighborhood is pet-friendly. Kids also support the essential civic institutions cities need to thrive, especially public schools.

But developers today are mostly great at building two things: apartment buildings and mass planned single-family communities. They are not good at building the “missing middle” housing, the formats that actually fit the life stage when people are deciding whether they can stay in their neighborhood and start a family.

That’s the gap I want to fill.

I’m designing and building homes specifically for couples who love their neighborhood and want to feel comfortable enough to stop trying not to have kids:
Small 3BR/2BA rowhouses, 2BR/1BA apartments.

Baby Maybe housing: Homes with just enough space, one extra room, and the confidence that you could have a baby without being forced to leave everything you’ve built your life around.

And after that first baby becomes a toddler, the decision for a family to stay will depend on schools, parks, transit, childcare, and safety. But in that crucial first stage, when babies are small and when a couple is asking whether parenthood fits into city life, having the right kind of home can be literally life-changing.

Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.

For thousands of years, cities have used shallow buildings, shared party walls, and interior courtyards to create dense housing with light, air, privacy, and usable outdoor space. In a contemporary courtyard block, these same principles make it possible to produce family-sized apartments with abundant daylight, cross-ventilation, generous floor plans, and direct access to patios, balconies, terraces, play areas, gardens, and shared yards, WITHOUT requiring every family to buy and maintain a detached house on scarce, expensive urban land.

Courtyard housing has appeared repeatedly during periods of urban expansion, from ancient Rome to the great apartment districts of late-19th- and early-20th-century Europe. The last major flourishing of this form came when Western European cities were facing rapid urban growth and rising demand for better housing in the city.

Something is breaking in America’s cities, and you can see it in empty classrooms.

New York City lost 22,000 students in one year. Chicago is down nearly 22 percent since 2011. Houston lost 8,300 students this year alone. Denver, Seattle, San Francisco, all bleeding families. Parents are not staging protests. They are just quietly leaving.

This is what abandonment looks like in real life. Working parents pulling their kids out because the schools feel unsafe, chaotic, or useless. Kids falling behind in reading and math. Districts admitting enrollment is collapsing while insisting everything is fine.

Nearly half of New York’s public school students can’t read or do math at grade level. Let that sink in. That is not a political talking point. That is a human disaster.

So families do what families always do. They protect their children. They choose charters. They choose homeschooling. They choose online schools. They scrape together money for private schools. Not because they hate public education, but because they love their kids more than they trust the system.

And what do cities do in response? They hire marketing firms to “recruit” students like customers. More kids means more funding. Fewer kids means budget cuts. So now school districts are competing for bodies instead of fixing what is broken.

This is the quiet collapse no one wants to name. Not war, not riots. Just parents walking away from a system that stopped working for their children.

You don’t lose 117,000 students in New York since 2019 because of birth rates alone. You lose them because trust is gone.

When families flee your schools, it means something deeper than policy failed.

text:
The problem with single-family housing in very high-cost parts of cities is that we're using very expensive land to house too few households.

In high-demand parts of the city, even a modest single-family home on a standard lot can sell for well over $1M (like this one that just went up around us). That means one household is carrying the full cost of very costly urban land. 

Apartments are so useful because they spread that land cost across many households, which is often the only way middle-income families can realistically afford to live in these locations.

Take a ~5,000 sq ft site worth about $1.4M.
Today , that site might hold two single-family homes selling for $1M+ each. If each home has 4 bedrooms, that is about 8 bedrooms total.

But if the same site were built as a 5–6 story courtyard-style apartment building, it could potentially support 10–16 homes (mix of larger and smaller apartments). 

Consider the relative land cost per bedroom:

Single-family scenario
Two homes on a ~5,000 sq ft site
Land value: ~$1.4M
About 8 bedrooms total
….roughly $175,000 in land cost per bedroom

Mid-rise apartment scenario
Same ~$1.4M land cost spread across 12 units
Assume mostly 3-bedroom units
About 36 bedrooms total
….roughly $39,000 in land cost per bedroom

That is about a 4–5x difference in land cost per bedroom before even getting into building efficiency, shared infrastructure, or reduced parking.

AND with the right building form (shallow floor plates, dual-aspect layouts, accessible shared courtyards, real foyers, family-sized kitchens, and usable green space) apartments can be nice family homes.

When the school board agrees to bring algebra back to middle school, kids shouldn’t have to wait two years.

That’s why Prop G remains relevant and necessary. Parents deserve to be heard. Kids in San Francisco deserve the same algebra already taught in nearly every Bay Area city.

The school board voted to bring back algebra piecemeal by the 2026-27 school year, giving the superintendent leeway to figure out how to do it. One proposal is to limit an algebra pilot to only a third of middle schools next year. The rest would get algebra after two years. That means most of today’s 6th graders are out of luck. Kids who are not part of the pilot would have to take algebra during summer school or online. Parents don’t trust the implementation promise over multiple years because they have seen school board plans go off the rails too often before.

The school district wouldn’t have even come this far to bring algebra back without the political pressure of Prop G. When I first proposed the measure, the school district quickly announced the formation of a committee to restore algebra in middle school. They hoped Prop G would go away. But I put algebra on the ballot with 10 of 11 supervisors because the school district needs the political pressure to do the right thing and be held accountable. The district had delayed bringing algebra back to 8th grade after knowing for many years that the decade-long ban was a failed policy.

The policy didn’t help kids who were behind in math. It only held back kids who love math. And we lost many of those kids when their parents pulled them out of public school.

Every resident of San Francisco should care about algebra because well-run public schools are essential for a city to function and thrive. Public school enrollment is in decline and families leave San Francisco for a number of reasons like public safety and education. Our future depends on keeping families here and algebra is a key part of the equation.

Bringing algebra back is a policy that could generate more school funding because when more families return to public schools for algebra, enrollment will increase along with state funding tied to the number of students. Nearly 30 percent of kids in San Francisco are in private school compared to the state average of just 10 percent. Offering 8th grade algebra could help reverse that trend as San Franciscans often give up on public schools as their kids reach middle school.

While only the school board can change its own policies, Prop G is important because parents deserve to have their voice heard loud and clear at the ballot box. Voters deserve to tell school leaders there is a mandate for 8th grade algebra and a robust math curriculum for students at all grade levels.

Prop G also lets San Franciscans send a very public message: Anyone running for school board in November must know that parents won’t settle for anything less than what a vast majority of Bay Area school districts already offer.

That’s why we’re rallying to bring algebra back.

If a kid likes math, let’s encourage it!

text:
Suburbs, remote work and dispersion as answers
Cities are the lifeblood of economies, and people will keep pouring into them. Yet birthrates are far below replacement in most countries and trending lower still, with economically vital cities being the literal center of this demographic decline.

How can we deal with this contradiction? It seems like suburbs hold one key: A way to be connected to the economy and family life at the same time. We saw how Australia's single-family-home suburbs have twice the fertility of its downtowns.

The urge to build urban apartment towers is strong, but these buildings will hurt fertility for generations to come. A house with a yard is dramatically better for families. In a rush to alleviate a short-time housing crunch, we risk harming birth rates even more in the long term.

Remote work and companies locating away from cities is even better: a way to let people live and support themselves in family-friendly places.

Of course, density is plainly not the only factor causing low fertility. Culture matters tremendously, and I talk about culture a great deal.

But how we build and live is so significant for birth rates and has impacts that are so long lasting, that we can't ignore it.

10/10
(Follow @MoreBirths for more on how we can solve our greatest crisis.)

“Cities shouldn’t just be great for the ambitious and adventurous at 25. They should be places where those same people can build a life at 35, too.”

This is so on point. Many Americans rightly think cities aren’t for families…but that’s because we stopped BUILDING them for families.

And while I do appreciate much of the YIMBY message (net good), I also think we need to be critical about what KIND of housing we are building. Not all housing is good housing. 

A city of only multi-family apartment buildings (as they’re built today) isn’t a city. It’s a collection of human storage units. 

That’s not to say big apartments are bad. But that ONLY big apartments are bad (which is virtually all new housing construction outside of suburban homes). 

Cities need design, beauty and humanity etched into every nook and cranny we can. And part of that beauty and humanity is incorporating children and families. 

Anecdotal, but something I’ve noticed holds generally true: If you make a place cool for kids and their parents (where both enjoy being there) it suddenly becomes a place for everyone—even the teens, singles and empty-nesters. I think there is something about having children around that can be life-giving and wholesome and bring out the best in people. 

To conclude: 

1) Hardware dictates what kind of software can run, and we’ve built hardware that’s incompatible for families in our cities.  

2) The built world is the human habitat. We shouldn’t treat it so flippantly as to simply say “anything that adds housing is good”. We actually do need GOOD housing. 

That doesn’t make it easy, and we shouldn’t be puritanical about it. There are real obstacles and limitations, and progress isn’t linear. But it SHOULD be the vision.

hi I am agnostic about the relationship between urbanization and fertility.

My understanding is that normal urban density levels are NOT negatively correlated with fertility when you control for housing size (ie, women living in 4BDs in the city are having as many kids as women living in 4BDs in the suburbs).

And I suspect that all cities need to do to increase the number of families with young kids  is to add enough family-sized housing to meet demand and bring down cost of a 3BD+.

That said, I do think there is a plausible secondary effect. If the centers of economic and cultural life (cities) become more visibly and functionally family-friendly, then having children may begin to feel more compatible & aspirational within a wider range of adult lifestyles, leading to more births. 

Ie, currently society tells adults that becoming a parent means moving away from centers of society, and buying a house with a  yard in a drive-everywhere suburb. For many 20 somethings, that sounds baaad. It did for me -- I watched my mom spend her 30s and 40s driving me and my three sisters around suburban W Michigan, and I wanted nothing to do with that. 

Obviously, suburban parenting appeals to many adults and that's wonderful.  (and there is a wide variety of suburbs, some requiring less car time than others) The problem is not the suburbs. Problem is that, for many adults who prefer cities, the urban alternative is artificially constrained because regulations and design culture restricts development of  3BD+ in small buildings with yard access.

Hence, my argument that cities should legalize and facilitate more family-friendly development in cities to accommodate the substantial share of adult population who prefers to raise kids in the city, if they can find suitable housing.

More broadly, I am interested in restoring the "complete life cycle, multigenerational" character of cities. Great civilizations have historically unfolded in cities where people lived over many generations, forming deep ties with local communities and institutions.  That multi-generational character has been broken in 20th century America, as a combination of bad urban development and car culture has pushed middle class families into suburbs.

It would be great for cities, for families, and for the country generally if more families had the option of staying in cities.

In other words, I am not trying to solve the fertility problem. I'm trying to solve a deeper civilizational problem, which is that our economic, cultural, and political centers of society do not accommodate residents across the life cycle.

Someone asked me what the future of Toronto looks like on the current trajectory. My answer was: "A city of fewer, richer families and where there is population growth its mostly in single people". Unless that is, we seriously review the building code.

Why? I mean, question: Where are the urban apartments that compete with houses in terms of space and value? Where are the apartments that make families feel kids could grow up there, or that make downsizers feel they’ve upgraded by moving to age?

Is there any housing that is *land-efficient* (ie an apartment,) yet aspirational for the two demographics who still feel the pull of the house? ie young families and older homeowners? Is there an aparmtnt that offers better value than a house? If we’ve chosen to be a city with growth boundaries (the Greenbelt) and a fixed number of houses, what happens as the city grows and families form?  Musical chairs with fewer chairs? Or do we review code, to expand the typologies developers can build?

This condition gets even more more intense as some houses are chopped into EHON sixplexes or demolished for short towers made of hotel-like, double-loaded corridors. Isn’t this all a formula for a city of as I was imagining, "fewer, richer families and more singles"? 

All fine, but what if you aren't super rich by age thirty and dare to want children? and a job? At the same time!? What's the plan? What if you want a nice apartment, but can't afford that ever increasing cost of houses- that didn't really come down even in the big burst of 2025? Why is the province not getting serious pressure to open a building code path for fire safe, apts and allows developers to build aspirational higher value space that's cheaper than a house, but nicer than current codos? space that's land efficient yet better than the double loaded, hotel-like corridors they narrowly allow? 

If we want to seriously address this problem,  it's *not* primarily a planning question, it's mostly in the building code.  It is the Ontario Building Code issued by Ontario's Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, and the Alternative solutions reviewed by the Chief Building Official. Single stair buildings that are fire safe, and have small, global standard elevators for people who intend to age and parents with strollers. 

Until there is review of the building code, we're lying to our selves about the core reason we need the "missing middle" in the first place. Till then we are fooling our selves to think that chopped up houses and short expensive towers are addressing this problem of rigid typology. Building code is core.

A good city however isn't determined by backyards or density of children. Those are only two dimensions. It also needs to be dense enough to have schools within walking distance (at least up to, but preferably including, college), shops, workplaces, services, including churches and sanctuaries. A city has to be somewhat sustainable, both in terms of economy and fertility. It is not difficult to build a new development to maximize backyards, but we also need to consider what that development will look like in 15 or 35 or 50 years. Suburbia with a lot of backyards might not be the best place to grow old in, when you need less play space and more clinics, for example.

This where the tricky part comes in. Traditionally this was solved in cities with hierarchies and common patterns: taller buildings and commercial space fronting the street, lower buildings and quiet space in the back or inside the courtyard blocks. Townhouse vs. Courtyard. So far no other urban form has been so long lived and successful.

Our modern experiment in cars and zones will not be long lived. In fact, it is already on its way out in large parts of the world.
